about: Oldest things of the isles in writing, books and letters: the first inscriptions, manuscripts, poems, letters and diaries, printing, newspapers and libraries, each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Bloomberg writing tablets
entries.age_text: AD 50–80; the earliest dated 8 January AD 57
entries.claim: The oldest handwritten documents known from Britain
entries.evidence: About 405 waxed writing tablets were excavated in the City of London in 2010–13 for Bloomberg's European headquarters and deciphered by Roger Tomlin; one financial document is dated 8 January AD 57, and another tablet carries the earliest written reference to London. They displaced the Vindolanda tablets (c. AD 100), long described as Britain's oldest handwritten documents. Earlier inscriptions exist on Iron Age coins, but these are the oldest handwriting.

sources.title: Bloomberg tablets
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The tablets are the earliest written documents found in Britain, dating from 50 to 80 AD in the early Roman period.

entries.name: Bath curse tablets
entries.claim: Two of the tablets may be written in a British Celtic language; if so they would be the only surviving writing in ancient British Celtic
entries.evidence: About 130 curse tablets of lead or pewter were thrown into the sacred spring of Sulis Minerva at Bath and recovered in excavations of 1978–83; nearly all are in British Latin. Two use Roman letters for a language that is not Latin and may be British Celtic, but there is no scholarly agreement on how to read them. One tablet also holds what UNESCO calls the earliest known reference to Christianity in Britain.

sources.title: Bath curse tablets
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: may be in a British Celtic language. If this should be the case, they would be the only examples of a written ancient British Celtic language; however, there is not yet scholarly consensus on their decipherment

sources.author: UK National Commission for UNESCO
sources.locator: Memory of the World UK Register, 2014
sources.quote: One tablet is currently unique in that it is believed to be made up of Celtic words written in the Latin alphabet. Another curse tablet contains what is currently the earliest known reference to Christianity in Britain.

entries.name: Ogham stones
entries.age_text: c. 4th century AD (on linguistic grounds, 4th–7th century)
entries.claim: The earliest writing in Ireland, and the oldest record of the Irish (Goidelic) language
entries.evidence: Ogham, an alphabet of strokes cut along the edge of a stone, was used on over 400 surviving memorial stones in Ireland and western Britain, most of them in southern Munster. The earliest are dated to about the 4th century, though the Heritage Council gives the 4th to 7th century on linguistic grounds; a 1st-century BC origin has been proposed without evidence. Their language, Primitive Irish, is known only from these inscriptions, mostly personal names.

sources.title: Ogham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Archaeological evidence shows that the earliest inscriptions in ogham date to about the 4th century AD, but James Carney believed its origin is rather within the 1st century BC

sources.title: Primitive Irish

entries.name: Cadfan Stone
entries.evidence: A cross-carved stone pillar in St Cadfan's Church, Tywyn, with four short memorial inscriptions in Old Welsh. Its date is disputed: Ifor Williams put it in the 8th century, Kenneth Jackson in the late 7th or early 8th, and Nancy Edwards firmly in the 9th, which the Royal Commission follows. Whatever the date, its inscriptions are the earliest known Welsh writing beyond names.

sources.title: Cadfan Stone, St Cadfan's Church, Tywyn (NPRN 302689)
sources.author: Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (Coflein)
sources.quote: Both sides of the stone are inscribed with a total of four inscriptions, which are the earliest known examples of written Welsh and the only early medieval inscriptions (other than names) in Old Welsh.

sources.title: Tywyn – St Cadfan's Church

entries.name: Cathach of St Columba
entries.claim: The oldest surviving manuscript from Ireland
entries.evidence: A Latin psalter, 58 leaves of an original of about 110, traditionally copied by St Columba (Colum Cille, died 597) and carried into battle by the O'Donnells as a talisman. Wikipedia dates it to the late 6th century; the Royal Irish Academy catalogue gives 600–699 and modern scholarship doubts the attribution to Columba himself. Either way it is the oldest Irish manuscript to survive, and the earliest Irish copy of the Gallican psalter.

sources.title: Cathach of St. Columba
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is a late 6th century Insular psalter. It is the oldest surviving manuscript in Ireland, and the second oldest Latin psalter in the world

sources.title: MS 12 R 33: The Cathach

sources.quote: is one of the oldest surviving manuscripts from Ireland, and although badly damaged, enjoys a unique status

entries.name: St Cuthbert Gospel
entries.claim: The earliest surviving intact European book, with the earliest Western bookbinding to survive
entries.evidence: A pocket Gospel of St John in Latin, probably made at Monkwearmouth-Jarrow, placed in St Cuthbert's coffin and removed at Durham in 1104. Its tooled red goatskin binding is original, which is what makes it the oldest intact book: older manuscripts survive only without their first bindings. The British Library bought it in 2012 (Add MS 89000).

sources.title: St Cuthbert Gospel
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Its finely decorated leather binding is the earliest known Western bookbinding to survive

sources.title: St Cuthbert Gospel

entries.name: Book of Deer
entries.age_text: 10th century; Gaelic notes added in the early 12th century
entries.claim: Possibly the oldest surviving manuscript made in Scotland, and its notes the earliest surviving Gaelic writing from Scotland
entries.evidence: A small Latin gospel book of the 10th century, at Deer in Aberdeenshire when monks added notes on land grants in Gaelic in the early 12th century. The notes are the earliest Gaelic surviving from Scotland. Whether the book itself is the oldest manuscript made in Scotland depends on the Book of Kells, which may have been begun on Iona.

sources.title: Book of Deer
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It contains the earliest surviving Gaelic writing from Scotland.

sources.title: Book of Deer
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It may be the oldest surviving manuscript produced in Scotland (although see Book of Kells)

sources.title: The Book of Deer

sources.quote: It therefore preserves the earliest writing in Scottish Gaelic that survives.

entries.name: Cædmon's Hymn
entries.age_text: composed 658–680 (if Bede is right); earliest copy c. 734–737
entries.claim: Claimed to be the oldest surviving English poem; the earliest securely datable Old English verse
entries.evidence: Nine lines in praise of God the Creator, which Bede says the cowherd Cædmon sang at Whitby. If Bede is right it was composed between 658 and 680, and its copy at the end of the Moore Bede (c. 734–737, Cambridge University Library) is among the earliest Old English poetry written down. The runic verses on the Ruthwell Cross and the Franks Casket are rival candidates for the oldest English poem.

sources.title: Cædmon's Hymn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The poem has a claim to being the oldest surviving English poem: if Bede's account is correct, the poem was composed between 658 and 680

sources.title: Cædmon's Hymn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the poem is the earliest securely dateable example of Old English verse

entries.name: Y Gododdin
entries.age_text: set c. 600; composed between the 7th and early 11th century; only manuscript 13th century
entries.claim: One of the oldest surviving poems in Welsh, often called the earliest
entries.evidence: A series of elegies for the warriors of the Gododdin who fell at Catraeth about 600, ascribed to the bard Aneirin and preserved only in the Book of Aneirin, written in the second half of the 13th century. The date of composition is disputed: a 7th-century origin in the Old North (now southern Scotland) is the traditional view, while others place it in Wales in the 9th to 11th century. Poems attributed to Taliesin are its rivals for the oldest Welsh poetry.

sources.title: Y Gododdin
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Book of Aneirin manuscript is from the later 13th century, but Y Gododdin has been dated to between the 7th and the early 11th centuries.

sources.title: Y Gododdin
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Even a 9th-century date would make it one of the oldest surviving Welsh works of poetry.

sources.title: The Llyfr Aneirin and the place-names of Y Gododdin
sources.author: Kelly A. Kilpatrick, Scottish Place-Name Society
sources.quote: However, the LA — the only manuscript to preserve the corpus — dates to the thirteenth century. This is a large chronological gap, and opinions on the antiquity of Y Gododdin are divided.

sources.title: Y Gododdin, the Votadini, and Arthurian Legend
sources.author: Medievalists.net
sources.quote: It is the earliest surviving Welsh poem, also known as the “Book of Aneirin.”

entries.category: Oldest letter, diary or personal writing
entries.name: Claudia Severa's birthday invitation (Vindolanda tablet 291)
entries.claim: One of the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman
entries.evidence: An ink letter on a thin wooden leaf from the fort of Vindolanda near Hadrian's Wall, in which Claudia Severa invites Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday. A scribe wrote most of it, but the closing greeting is in Severa's own hand, which makes it almost certainly the earliest known Latin written by a woman. The Vindolanda letters were once the oldest handwritten documents known from Britain; the Bloomberg tablets from London are now older.

sources.title: Vindolanda tablets
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The invitation is one of the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman.

sources.title: Tab.Vindol. 291. Birthday Invitation of Sulpicia Lepidina
sources.author: Roman Inscriptions of Britain
sources.quote: Almost certainly, therefore, these are the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman.

entries.category: Oldest letter, diary or personal writing
entries.name: Paston Letters
entries.claim: The earliest surviving great collection of private letters in English
entries.evidence: About a thousand letters and papers of the Paston family, Norfolk gentry, written during the Wars of the Roses and the early Tudor years; most are in the British Library. Smaller fifteenth-century family collections survive (the Stonor, Cely and Plumpton letters), so the claim rests on the size of the Paston archive rather than on any single letter being the oldest.

sources.title: Paston Letters
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Paston Letters are a collection of correspondence between members of the Paston family of Norfolk gentry and others connected with them in England between the years 1422 and 1509.

sources.title: How to read the Paston Letters #1
sources.author: Helen Castor
sources.quote: The Paston Letters are the earliest surviving great collection of private letters in the English language.

sources.title: The Paston Letters
sources.author: Friends of the National Libraries

entries.category: Oldest letter, diary or personal writing
entries.name: Diary of Lady Margaret Hoby
entries.claim: The earliest known diary written by a woman in English
entries.evidence: Margaret Hoby (1571–1633) of Hackness in Yorkshire kept a diary of religious exercises, household and estate business for six years; the manuscript, imperfect at both ends, is British Library Egerton MS 2614. Earlier diaries by men survive, and the claim is only that hers is the earliest known by an Englishwoman.

sources.title: Lady Margaret Hoby
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hers is the earliest known diary written by a woman in English.

sources.title: Margaret, Lady Hoby
sources.author: Catalogue of English Literary Manuscripts 1450–1700 (CELM)
sources.quote: A diary, covering the period from 9 August 1599 to 21 July 1605, in a single somewhat ungainly, largely italic hand, presumably autograph.

entries.name: Caxton's first printing at Westminster
entries.age_text: indulgence dated 13 December 1476; Dictes completed 18 November 1477
entries.claim: The first printing in England: a letter of indulgence (1476), and The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres, the first dated book printed in England (1477)
entries.evidence: William Caxton, who had already printed in English at Bruges, set up the first press in England in the Almonry at Westminster in 1476. The earliest known piece of his printing there is a letter of indulgence dated 13 December 1476, found at the Public Record Office in 1928; his Canterbury Tales was probably his first book there but is undated, so the Dictes of 18 November 1477 is the first dated book printed in England.

sources.title: Printing in England from William Caxton to Christopher Barker
sources.author: University of Glasgow Library
sources.quote: The first known piece of printing done in England, a Letter of Indulgence by John Sant, Abbot of Abingdon, with the date of purchase 13 December 1476, issued from this press.

sources.title: Printing in England from William Caxton to Christopher Barker

entries.name: Chepman and Myllar Prints
entries.claim: The earliest surviving dated book printed in Scotland
entries.evidence: Walter Chepman and Androw Myllar set up Scotland's first press in the Cowgate of Edinburgh under a royal charter of 1507. A single volume in the National Library of Scotland holds eleven pieces of early printing, each known only from that copy, including Lydgate's The Complaint of the Black Knight, completed on 4 April 1508.

sources.author: UK National Commission for UNESCO

sources.quote: include the earliest surviving dated book printed in Scotland: John Lydgate’s The Complaint of the Black Knight, completed by Walter Chepman and Androw Myllar in the Cowgate of Edinburgh on 4 April 1508

sources.title: Chepman and Myllar Press

sources.quote: The Chepman and Myllar Press was the first printing press to be established in Scotland.

entries.name: The London Gazette
entries.age_text: first published 7 November 1665 as The Oxford Gazette (other accounts: 14 or 16 November)
entries.claim: Claims to be the oldest surviving English newspaper and the oldest continuously published newspaper in the UK
entries.evidence: The Gazette began at Oxford, where Charles II's court had fled the plague, and took its London title in February 1666; it is still the official journal of record. Berrow's Worcester Journal, traced to the Worcester Post-Man of 1690, claims to be the oldest newspaper in continuous production, and the Stamford Mercury makes a similar claim, so the title depends on what counts as a newspaper. Sources disagree on the day of the first issue.

sources.title: The London Gazette
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The London Gazette claims to be the oldest surviving English newspaper and the oldest continuously published newspaper in the UK, having been first published on 7 November 1665 as The Oxford Gazette.

entries.name: Chetham's Library
entries.claim: The oldest public library in the English-speaking world (the oldest free public reference library)
entries.evidence: Founded under the will of the Manchester merchant Humphrey Chetham (1580–1653) in the medieval buildings of the collegiate church, and in continuous use since 1653. Older libraries survive in cathedrals, colleges and universities, but they were not open to the public; the claim is to be the oldest public one.

sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is the oldest free public reference library in the English-speaking world

sources.title: Chetham's Library

sources.quote: The library has been in continuous use since 1653.

sources.quote: The oldest public library in Britain

entries.name: Marsh's Library
entries.age_text: building 1701–05; established by Act of Parliament in 1707
entries.claim: The first public library in Ireland
entries.evidence: Built beside St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, for Archbishop Narcissus Marsh and incorporated by an Act of the Irish Parliament in 1707, under which it is still governed. Earlier Irish libraries belonged to the university or to churches; Marsh's was the first open to anyone able to read.

sources.title: Marsh's Library
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: When it opened to the public in 1707 it was the first public library in Ireland.

sources.title: The History of the Library
sources.author: Marsh's Library
sources.quote: as the first public library in Ireland. Although there were earlier libraries, they were either in the university or in churches.
